You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The bug report specifies that the MultiDirectional optimizer's iterateSimplex method loops forever when started exactly at the correct solution. Inspecting the method iterateSimplex reveals that it contains a while(true) infinite loop without an explicit convergence or stopping criterion other than returning early in some cases.

Within iterateSimplex, the algorithm performs steps typical of the Nelder-Mead simplex method: reflection, expansion, and contraction. For each step, after evaluating new potential simplices, it compares the new points with the best point using a comparator. If the reflected point is better, it tries expansion and returns after accepting a simplex; if not, it tries contraction and returns after acceptance.

However, when the starting point is the exact maximum, the reflection step will neither improve nor decrease the function value compared to the best (the starting point). This means the conditions to proceed and return early (inside the ifs for reflection or contraction) are never met. Consequently, none of the "return" statements inside the infinite loop executes, causing an indefinite loop.

The method evaluateNewSimplex performs generation of the transformed simplex points by linear transformation and evaluates them, but does not contain convergence checks itself.

No convergence check (e.g., checking if the change between iterations is below a threshold or if a certain metric for convergence is met) exists in iterateSimplex to break the endless while(true) loop if no improvement or contraction occurs.

Hence, when starting the optimizer exactly at the maximum, the algorithm's reflection and contraction do not improve the solution, so the flow never reaches any return statement, causing an infinite loop.

This diagnosis aligns with the bug report that suggests the infinite loop in iterateSimplex occurs without convergence checks and that the existing "while(true)" should be replaced by a convergence check to halt the iteration.

The test that fails invokes optimize with a maximum position, so this case of starting optimizations exactly at the correct maximum triggers the infinite loop issue.

Potential focus points to fix are in the iterateSimplex method, specifically adding or replacing the infinite loop with proper convergence or termination condition checks.

Summary: The infinite while(true) loop inside MultiDirectional.iterateSimplex lacks a convergence or termination condition. When the algorithm is started exactly at the optimum, reflection and contraction steps do not yield improvement, so none of the exit conditions inside the loop trigger, resulting in an infinite loop. The fix is to add suitable convergence checks to safely terminate the iteration.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
